---------- CONTENT ----------
This course introduces various concepts in the world of IT, from its historical breakthroughs to computer components and how they work, to the rise of the Internet and how data is transferred, and to how modern-day AI works in general. Basically, to anyone who is familiar with the HKDSE ICT subject (though, admittedly, my knowledge is from the "old" ICT curriculum, before they changed it in the 2025 HKDSE exams), this course's content will seem quite familiar to you, for instance in places like computer architecture (ALU, CU, etc.), protocols and how they transfer data packets, and data encryption (public keys, private keys, etc.).
The following list details what the course covers, across 10 lectures:
- Dawn of The Information Technology Revolution
- The Mystery of Electricity
- Digital Age: The Power of 0 & 1
- The Amazing Chip
- The Silicon Revolution
- Five Generations of Computing
- Claude Shannon and Information Theory
- Wired and Wireless Communications
- Cryptography and Secrets of the Web
- Coding World
- The Internet and World Wide Web
Now that I've listed it out, actually they did change quite a few parts of this course from the previous years.
The content itself, is... fine. Honestly, the syllabus is fine to me. Not too bad. Kinda boring and kinda useless. They could've gotten more in depth for numerous topics, perhaps, but owing to the fact that this is a common core course (and being in the "Technology" area, meaning students from SENG, I believe, aren't even supposed to take courses like this, unless they took this as a free elective or to replace UxOP/CTDL... which is what I opted for), the instructors were probably limited on what they could do.
I mean, yes. I personally enjoy reading about scientific and technological discoveries and whatnot, but I'd typically just search all of this up on Wikipedia in my own time.
I had thought that this course, with all these topics, should appeal to my weird brain quite a lot, and thus decided to enroll into this course, ignoring the comments saying not to (that, and because it didn't seem like a difficult course to get good grades in). Well, HAHAHAHA. More on this in the TEACHING section (the majority of my issues with this course are with the teaching).

I will also attach resources to this review when I return.)

comment_teaching:
App Design:
App design refers to the process of creating the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) for mobile applications. 
1. User Research: Before starting the design process, it's essential to understand the target audience and their needs. User research helps in identifying user preferences, behaviors, and pain points.
2. Wireframing and Prototyping: Wireframing involves visualizing the app's layout and structure. It helps in planning the app's navigation and functionality. Prototyping involves building interactive mockups to test and validate design concepts.
3. UI Design: User interface design focuses on creating visually appealing and intuitive interfaces. It involves selecting colors, typography, icons, and other visual elements to create a cohesive, user-friendly design.
4. UX Design: User experience design focuses on enhancing user satisfaction and usability. It involves creating seamless user flows, optimizing interactions, and ensuring the app meets the user's goals.
5. Usability Testing: Usability testing involves evaluating the app's design by observing users' interactions and collecting feedback. It helps identify usability issues and refine the design accordingly.
3D Modeling:
3D modeling is creating a three-dimensional representation of objects or scenes using specialized software. Here are some areas where 3D modeling is widely used:
1. Animation and Visual Effects: 3D modeling is extensively used in the entertainment industry for creating animated films, video games, and visual effects. It involves creating realistic characters, environments, and special effects.
2. Product Design and Prototyping: 3D modeling is used in product design to create virtual prototypes and visualize concepts before manufacturing. It enables designers to test different variations and make necessary modifications efficiently.
3. Architecture and Interior Design: 3D modeling is employed in architecture and interior design to create virtual representations of buildings, interiors, and landscapes. It helps architects and designers visualize and present their ideas to clients.
4. Medical and Scientific Visualization: 3D modeling is used in the medical field to create anatomical models for surgical planning, prosthetics, and medical education. It is also used in scientific research for visualizing complex data and simulations.
5. Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR): 3D modeling plays a crucial role in creating immersive experiences in VR and AR applications. It involves building virtual environments and objects that users can interact with in real time.
By learning about app design and 3D modeling, you can acquire valuable skills that can open up exciting career opportunities in industries like software development, gaming, multimedia, architecture, and more.

course_name: The Smart Consumer - Uncovering the Hidden Story behind the Product Label
comment_content:
This course examines how everyday lifestyle choices—such as food, clothing, and product use—impact sustainability in the context of climate change and resource limitations. While many individuals aim to consume responsibly, unclear environmental claims, complex product compositions, and hidden production processes often make it difficult to assess the true sustainability of goods and services.
Using a product life-cycle approach, the course investigates what makes products sustainable or unsustainable. It also explores the psychological, social, and economic factors that influence consumer behavior and how these behaviors can be shifted toward more sustainable patterns. Through interactive exercises, discussions, and local case studies focused on consumption in Hong Kong, students gain insight into how businesses and governments can support informed and responsible consumer choices.

comment_teaching: The teaching quality is quite good. Professor Veronique Lafon-Vinais teaches at a very manageable, slow pace and explains concepts clearly. Because she breaks down the foundational aspects of financial systems without rushing, the lectures are super friendly and accessible for non-SBM (School of Business and Management) students who might not have a prior background in finance.
comment_grading:
The assessment scheme in the syllabus is broken down as follows:  
Mid-term Exam (Exam I): 25%  
Final Exam (Exam II): 25%  
Online Quizzes (4 total): 20% (5% each)  
Group Assignment & Peer Evaluation (2 total): 20% (10% each)  
Class Participation (via iPRS & discussions): 10%  
Honestly, the grading is really good and it is very easy to secure an A-range grade, especially for SBM students. I didn't have to put a massive amount of effort into studying for the mid-term and final exams; simply attending the lectures consistently is more than enough to handle the assessment papers. A huge plus is that the exams and quizzes are entirely multiple-choice (MCQ) or True/False format, which keeps the testing straightforward.
comment_workload: The workload for this course is super light. There are 4 online quizzes and 2 group assignments in total, but each assignment only took about 1 to 2 hours to complete. When it comes to exam revision, you don't need to overthink it. Just doing the exercises and the quiz are entirely enough to prepare you well.

comment_teaching:
The course content is delivered through lectures. There are also biweekly writing workshops which guide you in writing your essay.
LECTURES
The professor is clearly very passionate, but honestly I spent most of the lecture doing other stuff because I wasn't that interested in the content. If you are interested in the content, then I think you will enjoy her teaching, as I saw many people in the front were very engaged and always answered her questions.
WRITING WORKSHOPS
The writing workshops introduce you to argumentative techniques which you will use in your essay. They also teach you how to write an introduction, body paragraphs, do citations and more. It is quite interactive as you talk to your workshop tutor and the other students a lot.
My workshop tutor Suzan Stamper was quite good and encouraged interaction among students. Unfortunately, she always left giving feedback on our homework until the last minute. To illustrate, I only got my first homework while walking from the LC to the classroom. I guess in UST, everyone is a deadline fighter, even the faculty :P
comment_grading:
The essay basically determines your grade.
10% Workshop attendance

    Discuss course topics in a forum-like environment with your peers.
10% Workshop homework
20% Lecture quiz
    Covers everything discussed in the lectures.
50% Essay
[BONUS] 3% In-class iPRS
--
WORKSHOPS
Workshop attendance and homework is self-explanatory. Just attend the workshops and do the homework reasonably and you will get the score. The quality of your homework is not assessed, but I advise you to try your best to get more useful feedback from your tutor. There are some homework quizzes, but you have unlimited attempts.
My score: Full
--
ONLINE DISCUSSION
For online discussions, I just created one moderately long post (300-400ish words) for each topic, and replied to a few of the others' submissions.
My score: Not released
--
LECTURE QUIZ
The lecture quiz is annoying for people like me who aren't interested in the content, because it forces you to revise stuff. The actual questions themselves don't look difficult, but it is easy to get them wrong because there's always multiple answers which feel correct, and the smallest detail determines the correct answer.
Low LQ Med. UQ High | Mean
0 14 16 18 22 | 15.56
My score: 14.5/22
--
ESSAY
900 - 1100 word argumentative essay discussing your viewpoint on a given essay prompt. There are 3 prompts to choose from this semester and you have to take a clear for-or-against stance.
You write the introduction and body paragraphs throughout the semester as part of your homework and you will get feedback. You then submit a draft essay, which is only graded on completion, but points will be deducted if certain criteria are not met. These criteria include:
- Outside word limit
- No humanities citations, DOI not included for journal entries
You then receive feedback on this draft and revise it. 1/3 of your essay score is based on how you respond to feedback, so take it seriously.
--
BONUS (iPRS)
Just attend the lectures and do the iPRS and you'll get the sweet bonus score.
--
Even though I got below mean on the lecture quiz, I still got an A, probably due to my essay. This shows that, as long as you perform decently on the lecture quiz (above LQ), your essay basically determines your score. The essay score is not released.
